title: Gut Microbiome Networks Across Schizophrenia, Major Depressive Disorder, and Bipolar Disorder: A Systematic Reanalysis and Machine Learning Study
content: Psychiatric disorders represent a leading cause of global disease burden, yet their accurate and timely diagnosis remains challenging due to incomplete understanding of etiology and a lack of objective pathognomonic features.  These factors leave diagnosis and treatment vulnerable to diagnostic errors. This diagnostic uncertainty, alongside emerging evidence linking the microbiota-gut-brain axis to psychiatric pathophysiology, has fueled the ongoing search for objective microbial biomarkers. We systematically searched PubMed and Scopus for gut microbiome 16S sequencing studies involving patients with schizophrenia (SCZ), major depressive disorder (MDD), and bipolar disorder (BD) that had publicly available sequencing read data. Data were extracted and analyzed through a harmonized bioinformatics pipeline to assess differences in α- and β-diversity and microbial composition. Co-occurrence networks were constructed, and differences in network topology, hubs, and taxon centrality were investigated. Finally, a random forest (RF) and a convolutional neural network ensemble (CNN) classifier were trained, and their performance in predicting diagnosis from microbiome composition was evaluated using two different cross-validation schemes. Analysis of 1402 samples from 17 studies revealed reduced α-diversity in MDD (q ≤ 0.0027) and significant β-diversity differences across groups (q ≤ 0.025), though these were largely accompanied by dispersion differences and extensive group overlap. MDD and SCZ exhibited depletion of butyrate-producing Lachnospiraceae, with SCZ additionally showing Actinobacteriota enrichment; BD exhibited no robust differential abundance. Network analysis showed higher modularity and lower density in SCZ—with MDD showing the inverse pattern—alongside increased centrality of taxa associated with neurotransmitter metabolism or inflammation across disorder groups, and decreased centrality of butyrate producers in MDD and SCZ. Classifiers performed well under 10-fold cross-validation (RF AUC = 0.856; CNN AUC = 0.862) but only modestly under leave-one-study-out cross-validation (RF AUC = 0.762; CNN AUC = 0.656). We identified a broad transdiagnostic signature of diminished butyrate-producer influence and increased prominence of taxa associated with neurotransmitter metabolism or inflammation. While machine learning demonstrates diagnostic potential, it is not yet ready for routine clinical application. Nevertheless, despite statistical significance, effect sizes were small, and group overlap was extensive, with study origin explaining far more variance than diagnosis. Echoing broader inconsistencies in the literature, these findings underscore the need to contextualize results and address criticisms of categorical diagnoses to avoid hyperbolic claims about microbial biomarkers or machine learning in psychiatry.
